title: His death, 1839
hook: when he died, several queens and servants burned on his pyre, against the Gurus' teaching

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maharani Jind Kaur, and your line, a brave queen. Today is a heavy day, so go gently with it.

The man who built the kingdom is old now. Strokes have taken much of his speech. In his last days, tradition says, he gave away gifts and treasure, and his court gathered around him in Lahore. Then the Lion of the Punjab died, and the city mourned. What happened at his funeral is part of this story, and Sikh histories tell it honestly, because the Gurus had already spoken to it.
screen: `THE MAHARAJA GROWS OLD.` → `HIS COURT GATHERS IN LAHORE.` → `THE LION OF THE PUNJAB DIES.`

segments.voice: At his cremation, several of his queens and some serving women burned with him on the pyre. This was sati, an old custom in parts of India, in which a widow died on her husband's funeral fire. Histories record it, and Sikh tellings of it are full of sorrow. Long before, Guru Amar Das had spoken plainly. In a hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib, he says that women who burn themselves with their husbands' bodies are not truly called satis. The true sati, he says, is one who lives on in goodness and contentment, and honors the Lord. The Gurus spoke against the custom, and Sikh tradition remembers Guru Amar Das working to end it among his followers. So here is a hard thing. The kingdom ruled in the Khalsa's name, and yet at its founder's funeral, a practice the Gurus had rejected went ahead. An old custom was stronger, that day, than the Guru's word, and Sikh histories say plainly that the court fell short of the Gurus' teaching. You don't have to make a hard truth smaller, or make it the whole story either. The Maharaja who gave gold to the Harmandir and mercy to his enemies is the same man at whose funeral this happened. Both are true, and holding both is part of telling history with honesty.
screen: `QUEENS AND SERVANTS ON THE PYRE.` · `GURU AMAR DAS HAD SPOKEN AGAINST IT.` · `THE COURT FELL SHORT OF THE GURU.` · `HOLDING A HARD TRUTH.` · then, large: `EVEN KINGS FELL SHORT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the women who died that day, without names, just as people, and keep a moment of silence for them. Then, if you like, let a hard truth in a story you love sit beside what's good in it, without arguing and without hurrying past. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
His death. The end of the Maharaja's life, and the funeral where queens and servants died on his pyre, against what Guru Amar Das had taught.
Your line: even kings fell short. The good stays true, and so does this. See you tomorrow.
